# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is beneficial for those who want to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted, open-source solution, with the core use case being team collaboration and communication. The key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Element allows users to have full control over their data, whereas Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Slack is generally easier to set up, while Element requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Element can be more scalable due to its self-hosted nature, allowing users to add more resources as needed.
* Integration with external services: Element has a more limited set of integrations compared to Slack, which has a large library of third-party apps.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Large library of third-party integrations
* Good mobile app support
* Reliable and stable
* Limited control over data
### Element
* Self-hosted and open-source
* Full control over data
* Highly customizable
* Scalable
* Limited integrations with external services

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that need a simple, easy-to-use communication platform with a wide range of integrations. It's also suitable for teams that don't require full control over their data. Element, on the other hand, is ideal for larger teams or organizations that require a high degree of customization, scalability, and control over their data. It's also suitable for teams with technical expertise who can handle the setup and maintenance of a self-hosted solution.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack export tool, which provides a JSON file containing your team's messages, files, and other data.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it according to your needs.
3. Use the Element import tool to import your Slack data into Element.
4. Configure any necessary integrations and settings in Element.
5. Test your Element setup to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the features and polish of Slack. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's scalability can be limited by the resources available on the self-hosted server. However, for teams that require full control over their data and are willing to handle the setup and maintenance of a self-hosted solution, Element is a good choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need a wide range of integrations
* Teams that require full control over their data and are willing to handle self-hosting
* Organizations with existing technical expertise and resources
* Teams that don't need advanced features like screen sharing or video conferencing
* Users who prioritize data ownership and security over ease of use

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and open-source, and you can self-host it on your own server.
### Is Element as easy to use as Slack?
No, Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, especially for self-hosting.
### Can I integrate Element with external services?
Yes, Element has a growing library of integrations with external services, but it's not as extensive as Slack's.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can export your Slack data and import it into Element using the Element import tool.
### Is Element suitable for large teams?
Yes, Element is highly scalable and suitable for large teams, but it requires more technical expertise and resources.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are communication platforms designed for team collaboration, offering features such as messaging, file sharing, and integrations. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering a switch from Slack to Mattermost, possibly due to concerns over data ownership or costs. The core use case for both tools is to facilitate team communication and collaboration, with a key reason to switch being the desire for more control over data and lower costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, while Slack charges per user.
* Data Ownership: Mattermost allows for full data ownership, while Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup Complexity: Mattermost can be more complex to set up, especially for those without experience in self-hosting.
* Scalability: Both platforms are scalable, but Mattermost's self-hosted option gives more control over scalability.
* Integration with GitHub: Mattermost has native integration with GitHub, while Slack requires a third-party integration.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

### Slack
* Pros:
  + Easy to set up and use
  + Wide range of integrations available
  + Good mobile app support
  + Large user community
  + Regular updates with new features
* Cons:
  + Can be expensive for large teams
  + Limited control over data
  + Limited customization options
  + Can be distracting with many notifications
  + Limited self-hosting options
### Mattermost
* Pros:
  + Free, self-hosted option available
  + Full control over data
  + High customization options
  + Scalable and secure
  + Native integration with GitHub
* Cons:
  + Can be complex to set up, especially for those without experience in self-hosting
  + Limited mobile app support compared to Slack
  + Smaller user community compared to Slack
  + Limited support for some integrations
  + Requires more technical knowledge to manage

## When to Choose Each
### Slack
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations. It's suitable for small to medium-sized teams that don't mind the costs and are looking for a simple, user-friendly solution. Slack is also a good choice for teams that don't require full control over their data and are comfortable with a proprietary platform.
### Mattermost
Mattermost is a good choice for teams that require full control over their data and are looking for a self-hosted solution. It's suitable for large teams or organizations that want to avoid per-user costs and have the technical expertise to manage a self-hosted platform. Mattermost is also a good choice for teams that prioritize customization and scalability.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up a Mattermost server and configure it according to your needs.
3. Use the Mattermost import tool to import your Slack data, which supports JSON format.
4. Configure any necessary integrations and customize your Mattermost instance.
5. Test your Mattermost instance to ensure everything is working as expected.

Mattermost is a production-ready platform for most users, offering a wide range of features and a self-hosted option. However, it may not be suitable for teams that require a high level of support or a simple, user-friendly interface. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Mattermost requires a certain level of technical expertise to manage and customize. We recommend Mattermost for teams that prioritize data control and customization, while Slack may be a better choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations.

* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need many integrations and want to save on costs.
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that require full control over their data and are comfortable with self-hosting.
* Large teams (more than 50 users) that want to avoid per-user costs and have the technical expertise to manage a self-hosted platform.
* Teams that prioritize customization and scalability.
* Teams that don't need mobile app support and are comfortable with a web-based interface.

## FAQ

Yes, Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option. However, you'll need to consider the costs of hosting and maintaining your own server.
### Is Mattermost as easy to use as Slack?
No, Mattermost can be more complex to set up and use, especially for those without experience in self-hosting.
### Can I integrate Mattermost with other tools?
Yes, Mattermost offers a wide range of integrations, including native integration with GitHub.
### Is Mattermost secure?
Yes, Mattermost is designed with security in mind and offers features such as encryption and access controls.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Mattermost?
Yes, you can export your Slack data and import it into Mattermost using the Mattermost import tool.

# Discord vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Discord and Element are communication platforms designed for teams and communities. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and organizations looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted, open-source solution. The core use case for both tools is real-time communication, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Discord offers a free plan with limitations, while Element is completely free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Element allows users to own their data, whereas Discord stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Discord is relatively easy to set up, while Element requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Element is highly scalable, especially when self-hosted, whereas Discord's scalability is limited by its proprietary architecture.
* Integration: Element supports Matrix protocol, allowing for seamless integration with other Matrix-based platforms, whereas Discord has limited integration with external platforms.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Discord | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $9.99/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $4.99/month (Nitro subscription) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $4.99/month (Nitro subscription) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Discord:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Large user base and community
* Good quality voice and video chat
* Mobile apps available
* Limited control over data and customization
**Element:**
* Self-hosted and open-source
* High level of customization and control
* Supports Matrix protocol for integration
* Scalable and secure
* Steeper learning curve and technical requirements

## When to Choose Each
Discord is suitable for small to medium-sized teams or communities that prioritize ease of use and don't require high levels of customization or control over their data. Element, on the other hand, is ideal for larger organizations or teams that require self-hosting, high scalability, and customization, and are willing to invest time and resources into setup and maintenance.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Discord server data using the Discord API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it according to your needs.
3. Import your Discord data into Element using the Matrix protocol or a compatible import tool.
4. Configure any additional features or integrations required by your team.
5. Test and verify that all features are working as expected.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users due to its technical requirements and complexity. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's self-hosting requirements can be resource-intensive, and users may need to invest in dedicated servers or infrastructure. However, for teams that require high levels of customization and control, Element is a strong contender, and we recommend switching from Discord to Element if you have the technical expertise and resources to support it.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't require voice or video chat
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that prioritize customization and control
* Large organizations (over 100 users) that require self-hosting and scalability
* Communities that require high levels of security and encryption
* Developers or technical teams that can handle self-hosting and customization

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is completely free and open-source, with no costs or limitations.
### Is Element self-hosted?
Yes, Element can be self-hosted on your own servers, giving you full control over your data.
### Does Element support voice and video chat?
Yes, Element supports high-quality voice and video chat, as well as screen sharing and other collaboration features.

Yes, Element supports the Matrix protocol, allowing for seamless integration with other Matrix-based platforms.

Not necessarily, as Element's self-hosting and customization options can be beneficial for large gaming communities.

title: Notion vs Obsidian
comparison_markdown:
# Notion vs Obsidian

## Overview

All-in-one workspace combining notes, databases, wikis, and project management. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Obsidian is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Notion costs $8-$20/user/month; Obsidian is Free (local use)
- **License**: Notion is Proprietary; Obsidian is Proprietary (free personal)
- **Data ownership**: Obsidian can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Obsidian eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Obsidian has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Notion | Obsidian |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $8-$20/user/month | Free (local use) |
| License | Proprietary | Proprietary (free personal) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$400/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,600/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Notion

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Obsidian

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Notion if:** Notion is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Obsidian if:** Obsidian is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Notion in its standard export format, review Obsidian import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Obsidian is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Notion tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Obsidian instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Notion, switching to self-hosted Obsidian will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Notion until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Notion paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Obsidian free to use?
Yes. Obsidian is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Notion to Obsidian?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Notion data, follow the Obsidian import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Obsidian get regular updates?
Yes. Obsidian has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Obsidian without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Obsidian development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Notion](https://notion.so) and [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md) before making decisions.*

title: GitHub vs GitLab
comparison_markdown:
# GitHub vs GitLab

## Overview

GitHub is the world largest code hosting platform, owned by Microsoft, with 100 million developers. GitLab is a complete DevOps platform that can be fully self-hosted, offering everything from Git hosting to CI/CD and container registries.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub free tier is generous; GitLab Community Edition is fully free to self-host
- **CI/CD**: GitLab has more powerful built-in CI/CD pipelines; GitHub Actions is catching up
- **Self-hosting**: GitLab is designed to be self-hosted; GitHub Enterprise self-hosted is expensive
- **Feature scope**: GitLab is a complete DevSecOps platform; GitHub focuses on developer collaboration
- **Community**: GitHub has a dramatically larger open-source community and project discoverability

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### GitLab

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [gitlabhq/gitlabhq](https://github.com/gitlabhq/gitlabhq) * ~24k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub suits open-source projects wanting maximum community visibility or teams deeply integrated with GitHub Actions workflows.

**Choose GitLab if:** GitLab self-hosted is ideal for enterprises needing full control over their DevOps stack or regulated industries.

## Migration Path

GitLab provides a GitHub importer that migrates repositories, issues, PRs, wikis, and milestones. Update CI configuration from GitHub Actions to GitLab CI/CD YAML format.

## Our Take

GitLab is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your GitLab instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted GitLab will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is GitLab free to use?
Yes. GitLab is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to GitLab?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the GitLab import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does GitLab get regular updates?
Yes. GitLab has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use GitLab without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if GitLab development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [GitLab](https://gitlab.com) before making decisions.*
meta_description: GitLab is a free, self-hosted alternative to GitHub. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

title: GitHub vs Gitea
comparison_markdown:
# GitHub vs Gitea (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and Gitea are two popular Git repository management tools used for version control and collaboration. This comparison is beneficial for developers, teams, and organizations looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted, open-source solution or seeking more control over their data. The core use case for both tools is source code management, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more flexibility and autonomy over their repository.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers free accounts with limited features, while Gitea is completely free and open-source.
* Data ownership: Gitea allows users to self-host their repositories, giving them full control over their data, whereas GitHub stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: GitHub has a more streamlined and user-friendly setup process, while Gitea requires more technical expertise to set up and configure.
* Scalability: GitHub has better scalability and performance, thanks to its large infrastructure and resources, whereas Gitea's scalability depends on the user's server capabilities.
* Feature difference: GitHub has a more comprehensive project management feature set, including integrated issue tracking and project boards, whereas Gitea has a more minimalistic approach, relying on third-party integrations for additional features.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | Gitea |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**GitHub:**
* Pros:
	+ User-friendly interface and onboarding process
	+ Comprehensive project management features
	+ Large community and ecosystem of integrations
	+ Robust security and compliance features
	+ Scalable and performant infrastructure
* Cons:
	+ Limited control over data and repository management
	+ Costs can add up for large teams or organizations
	+ Proprietary license limits customization and flexibility
**Gitea:**
* Pros:
	+ Free and open-source, with full control over data and repository management
	+ Customizable and extensible through third-party integrations
	+ Lightweight and efficient, with low system requirements
	+ Active community and growing ecosystem of integrations
* Cons:
	+ Steeper learning curve and more complex setup process
	+ Limited project management features out of the box
	+ Scalability and performance depend on user's server capabilities
	+ Limited support for large-scale enterprises

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is suitable for large teams, enterprises, or organizations that require a comprehensive project management feature set, robust security and compliance features, and scalable infrastructure. It is also a good choice for users who prioritize a user-friendly interface and onboarding process. On the other hand, Gitea is ideal for small to medium-sized teams, individuals, or organizations that value flexibility, customization, and control over their data and repository management. It is also a good choice for users who are comfortable with a more minimalistic approach and are willing to invest time in setting up and configuring their repository.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub Archive format.
2. Set up a Gitea instance on your server, either manually or using a docker container.
3. Use the Gitea import tool to import your repository from the GitHub Archive format.
4. Configure any additional features or integrations you need, such as issue tracking or project boards.
5. Update any existing links or references to your repository to point to the new Gitea instance.

## Our Take
Gitea is a production-ready alternative to GitHub for many users, offering a high degree of customizability and control over data and repository management. However, it is essential to be aware of the technical limitations, such as the need for self-hosting and the potential for scalability issues. For teams and organizations that value flexibility and autonomy, Gitea is an excellent choice, but for those who require a comprehensive project management feature set and robust security and compliance features, GitHub may still be the better option.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that do not need comprehensive project management features
* Individuals or solo developers who value flexibility and control over their repository
* Organizations with limited budgets that cannot afford GitHub's per-user costs
* Teams that require customizability and extensibility through third-party integrations
* Users who prioritize data ownership and autonomy over their repository management

## FAQ
### Can I self-host Gitea on my own server?
Yes, Gitea is designed to be self-hosted, and you can run it on your own server or virtual private server.
### Is Gitea compatible with GitHub repositories?
Yes, Gitea supports importing repositories from GitHub using the GitHub Archive format.
### Does Gitea have a user-friendly interface?
Gitea's interface is more minimalistic and may require more technical expertise to navigate, but it is still user-friendly and intuitive.
### Can I use Gitea for large-scale enterprise projects?
While Gitea can be used for large-scale projects, it may not be the best choice due to its limited scalability and performance compared to GitHub.
### Is Gitea free?
Yes, Gitea is completely free and open-source, with no costs or licensing fees.

# Figma vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Figma and Penpot are two popular design and collaboration tools used by teams to create user interface (UI) and user experience (UX) designs. This comparison is beneficial for designers, product managers, and developers who are looking for a tool that meets their specific needs, particularly those considering switching from Figma to Penpot due to cost or data ownership concerns.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Figma offers a free plan with limited features, while Penpot is completely free and open-source.
* Data Ownership: Figma stores data on its servers, while Penpot allows users to self-host and maintain full control over their data.
* Setup Complexity: Figma has a more streamlined onboarding process, while Penpot requires more technical expertise to set up, especially for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Figma is designed to handle large teams and complex projects, while Penpot is still developing its scalability features.
* Feature Difference: Figma has a more comprehensive set of features, including advanced prototyping and collaboration tools, while Penpot has a stronger focus on open-source principles and community-driven development.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Figma | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $600-$3750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Figma
* Pros:
	+ Advanced features and tools
	+ Large community and user base
	+ Well-established and reliable
	+ Good customer support
* Cons:
	+ Expensive, especially for large teams
	+ Limited control over data
	+ Proprietary license
### Penpot
* Pros:
	+ Free and open-source
	+ Self-hosting option
	+ Community-driven development
	+ High customizability
* Cons:
	+ Limited features compared to Figma
	+ Steeper learning curve
	+ Limited scalability
	+ Limited customer support

## When to Choose Each
Figma is the better choice for large teams or enterprises that require advanced features, scalability, and reliability. It is also suitable for teams that prioritize ease of use and are willing to pay for it. On the other hand, Penpot is ideal for small to medium-sized teams, startups, or individuals who value data ownership, customizability, and cost-effectiveness. It is also a good choice for teams that are already familiar with open-source tools and have the technical expertise to set it up and maintain it.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Figma designs in SVG or PNG format.
2. Use the Penpot import tool to upload your designs.
3. Set up your Penpot instance, either self-hosted or using the cloud version.
4. Configure your team and user settings.
5. Test and refine your designs in Penpot.

## Our Take
Penpot is still a relatively new tool, and while it shows great promise, it may not be production-ready for most users right now. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Penpot's scalability features are still in development, which may affect large teams or complex projects. However, for small to medium-sized teams or individuals who value data ownership and customizability, Penpot is definitely worth considering, and we recommend switching from Figma if you don't require advanced features or scalability.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who don't need advanced features
* Startups or individuals who prioritize cost-effectiveness
* Teams that require self-hosting and data ownership
* Designers who value customizability and community-driven development
* Small to medium-sized teams who don't need scalability

## FAQ
### Can I use Penpot for free?
Yes, Penpot is completely free and open-source. You can use it without paying any fees, and you have the option to self-host it on your own servers.
### Is Penpot as feature-rich as Figma?
No, Penpot has a more limited set of features compared to Figma, but it is still a powerful design and collaboration tool.
### Can I import my Figma designs into Penpot?
Yes, Penpot has an import tool that allows you to upload your Figma designs in SVG or PNG format.
### Is Penpot suitable for large teams?
Not yet, Penpot's scalability features are still in development, and it may not be suitable for large teams or complex projects.
### Can I use Penpot for prototyping?
Yes, Penpot has basic prototyping features, but they are not as advanced as Figma's.
